source.title: Robust Neural Network Classification via Double Regularization
source.authors: Olof Zetterqvist; Rebecka Jörnsten; J. Jonasson

page_placements.theme: Regularization and capacity controls have setting-dependent effects

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text is garbled, but the relevant tables and descriptive text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates neural-network classification under simulated label corruption using a new observation-weighting objective and standard regularization comparisons. It does not reproduce fitting completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The paper studies partial label corruption, not completely random labels. The reported results concern test accuracy, training accuracy in one experiment, robustness to initialization, and label-weight identification. Cited findings from Zhang et al. (2016) and other prior work are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates a label-noise mitigation method. Its own results measure classification performance, initialization robustness and identification of mislabels, without establishing random-label memorization, perfect fitting across noise levels, or separate learning trajectories for real and noisy labels. The record's tests/T2 classification is therefore unsupported.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that DRFit preserves or improves classification accuracy, reduces overfitting and initialization sensitivity, and identifies mislabeled examples. Their early-stopping conclusion concerns ordinary parameter regularization under label noise; the transfer-learning experiment showed no overfitting for any compared method.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces DRFit, which combines parameter regularization with penalized observation weights; experiments compare it with ridge regularization and Mixup. It does not use the original random-label fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise distribution and level; class-specific scaling factors ρc; initialization; choice of regularization method. The paper reports sensitivity to initialization for ridge and notes performance can depend on α and ρc.

fits_no_version.finding: For binary CIFAR-10 with label noise, ridge test accuracy declines after its peak: 0.91690 to 0.82947 for 20/20 noise, 0.91790 to 0.83802 for 30/10, and 0.92814 to 0.82148 for 40/0. These averages exclude crashed runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter regularization can leave substantial late-training deterioration in generalization under partial label noise. Test deterioration alone does not establish noisy-label memorization or its timing relative to clean-label learning.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports training accuracies of 0.5426 for DRFit, 0.4978 for ridge and 0.4440 for Mixup in the transfer-learning experiment with 40% label noise. The authors report no overfitting in this experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The selected regularized transfer-learning models retain useful test performance without perfect training accuracy; this does not test convergence to perfect fit across a corruption sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: DRFit improves robustness and separates correctly labeled from mislabeled observations through learned observation weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Observation reweighting can mitigate partial label noise and identify suspect annotations.

record.problems: The experiments use selected label-noise settings rather than a full zero-to-all corruption sweep. Several performance trajectories are figure-only. In the binary CIFAR-10 experiment, crashed runs are removed from both DRFit and ridge for direct comparison; the paper notes that sensitivity to ρc remains for future study.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows qualify for the supplied claim versions: the experiments do not test complete random labels, fitting unstructured inputs, or the full noise sweep and training-fit behavior specified in V4. The reported partial-noise accuracy and weight-identification outcomes concern DRFit's robustness method, rather than the claim's random-label fitting behavior.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error and chance test performance with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption.
Training-set fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit as corruption increases and steady test-error degradation toward chance. The binary experiments compare clean data with three noise distributions having the same overall corruption fraction; the multiclass experiment uses only 40% noise.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent complete random-label fitting, and the effect of removing those regularizers on clean-label generalization.
Separate measurements showing real patterns learned before noisy labels. Test-accuracy trajectories and observation-weight separation do not establish that learning order.

record.verdict_notes: The empty result-row set is appropriate for these claim versions, although the record incorrectly marks V4 as tested. The related results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing claim-bearing rows.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling of the training set, zero or near-zero training error on it, and test error at chance without changing the original architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random labels and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels increases.

The experiments use selected partial-noise settings, not a sweep from zero to all labels corrupted. They do not report perfect training-set fit across those settings or a steadily rising test error toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels, and whether removing them alone impairs generalization on true labels.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and whether these labels are learned differently over training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The method builds on label-noise overfitting and early-stopping intuition, without testing complete-random-label fitting or separately measuring learning of real and noisy labels.

tranche.reason: DRFit uses the premise of eventual overfitting to noisy labels to motivate mitigation; its experiments measure classification performance and mislabel detection without establishing any supplied claim version.

source_check.notes: Section 6.1 and Table 2 confirm 40% noise in each class and training accuracies 0.5426, 0.4978 and 0.4440 for DRFit, ridge and Mixup. The accompanying text explicitly reports no overfitting for all three models.
